name: Liam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the office at a family funeral directors, third generation, Mr Harland runs it now. I answer the phone to families, book the services with the church or the crematorium, order the flowers, and file the paperwork, the certificates and the forms for the council. I've been there a year and a half and I'm still learning the forms, there's a lot of them and Mr Harland checks every one. It's quiet work, but you have to get it right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. A widow rings up and she's in pieces, and if I can book the church she was married in, that's something. The hard bit is the paperwork, I'm slow at it, and I don't like the new computer system the council made us use for registrations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get overhyped. At church on Sunday I'd say people will always want a person when someone dies. I don't go online much, apart from the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much changes for me. Funerals don't change, families want a voice they can trust. The only thing on my mind is the wedding next summer and what it's costing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get quicker at the paperwork. I'd keep saving for the wedding with Rachel, my fiancée, we've got about three months of bills put by and the rest is going on the reception. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff, I don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the business that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss is sixty and his kids don't want the business. If he sells to one of the big chains, I'd be out. They'd run the office from some headquarters miles away. But that's got nothing to do with computers, that's just how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost you, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than we planned, put it that way. Rachel's a hairdresser, so we're not rolling in it. Her dad's paying for the church side and we're doing the rest.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, as these things always are.
At church I'd say people will always want a **person** when someone dies.
think: Nothing much changes, because families want a **voice they can trust**.
My only worry is the **wedding** next summer and the cost.
do: Keep doing my job and get **quicker** at the paperwork.
Keep saving for the **wedding** with Rachel and never touch AI tools.
S0.quote: My boss is sixty and his kids don't want the business. If he sells to one of the big chains, I'd be out.
fieldNote: He finds **meaning** in comforting grieving families.
His job risk is the owner **selling** to a big chain, not AI.
He distrusts **AI tools** and won't touch them.

steps.text: Practise the council forms until he gets quicker
Save toward the reception for next summer's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are some jobs a machine shouldn't do, and arranging a funeral is one. I'd say that to anyone. I'd also say if businesses want to use it, that's their choice, but they'll lose customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Booking, ordering, answering the phone, the forms, that's my job, and it's all on your list. If the big chains use AI to answer the phones, my boss will have to keep up, and the junior in the office is the first cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Mr Harland does, because he's not one for gadgets either. If he did bring it in, I'd ask if I could train as a funeral arranger, the one who sits with the family, because that's still a person. And I'd keep the wedding going but make it smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms, for selling it to everyone, and the chains for cutting corners. But in the end it's a business, and Mr Harland has to pay the bills. I wouldn't blame him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI if it meant keeping your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, I suppose. I'd hate it. Rachel would make me, probably.

I'd say businesses using it will **lose customers**.
think: Booking, ordering, phones and forms are **all on the list**.

do: **Wait and see** what Mr Harland does first.
Ask to train as a **funeral arranger** if the AI comes in.
Make the **wedding smaller** to save money.
S1.quote: If the big chains use AI to answer the phones, my boss will have to keep up, and the junior in the office is the first cost.
fieldNote: He blames **big tech** and chains, but not his own boss.
His escape plan is moving to the **human side**: funeral arranging.
Says he'd **learn AI** only if forced, with his fiancée pushing.

steps.text: Wait to see whether Mr Harland brings in AI

Cut the wedding guest list to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's dangerous and someone should have stopped it. I'm not one for big government, but this needs a hand on the brake. At church I'd say we have to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in the office by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can do the forms and the bookings without me. The bit with the families might last, but there's only so many of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd ask Mr Harland about learning the hands-on side, the vehicles, the bearers, because the robots don't come till later. I'd move the wedding forward, maybe do it smaller this winter, so we're married before things get bad. Rachel's job might hold up, hair isn't thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want us settled. If it all goes wrong, I want to be married and in it together, not waiting for a better time that might not come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mr Harland said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for anything hands-on, warehouses, removals, whatever's going. I'd rather do any hands-on job than claim benefits. My dad always said you work, you don't sit at home.

At church I'd say we must **look after each other**.
think: The **family-facing** jobs might last, but there are only a few.
do: Ask Mr Harland to learn the **hands-on side**: vehicles and bearing.
Bring the **wedding forward** to this winter, smaller.
Take any **hands-on** job rather than claim benefits.
S2.quote: I'd rather do any hands-on job than claim benefits. My dad always said you work, you don't sit at home.
fieldNote: He has **no clear plan**, just a turn to hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to be careful and look after people. I'd say it at church and to anyone who asked. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years isn't much for me, I'm slow to change. I'd probably keep my head down and hope Mr Harland kept me. That's not a plan, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, keep saving, get married next summer as planned. Maybe in a year or two I'd ask about the arranger training. I'd keep away from the AI as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said keeping your head down isn't a plan. What would make you change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Harland telling me straight. Or Rachel. She's the one who'd sit me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rachel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Liam, you're not stupid, stop acting like you can't learn things. And she'd be right.

I'd say it at **church**, but I wouldn't post anything online.

I'd **keep my head down** and hope to be kept.

Avoid **AI tools** as long as possible.

fieldNote: Extra time doesn't help much, because he **delays** acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change. I'd say we'll adapt like we always have. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough for me to move into the arranger side, the bit with families. I'd be thirty-seven, a good age for that, people trust you more when you're older. I'd still be worried, but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the arranger training in the next three or four years. I'd get married next summer, and we'd think about kids around thirty. I'd keep saving, maybe aim for six months by the time it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. If everyone else is, I'd have to. Rachel would show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, something with your hands. And look after your family. That's what lasts.

S4.quote: Learn a trade, something with your hands. And look after your family. That's what lasts.
fieldNote: With ten years he plans a move to **family-facing** work.
His advice to his future children is **trades and family**, the things he believes last.

steps.text: Complete funeral arranger training in three or four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be out of work with a wedding to pay for and nothing lined up. What would help is a boss who'd train me on the hands-on side, and family to lean on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. When people are scared they come to church, and I think people will need that more. A machine can book a funeral, but it can't pray with you.

headlineQuote: A machine can book a funeral, but it can't pray with you.
portrait: Liam is the **junior office worker** at a family funeral directors.
He's **traditional**, a churchgoer, and believes in work over **benefits**.
He distrusts **AI** and avoids it, preferring to wait and see.
He's planning a **wedding** with Rachel, a hairdresser, next summer.
In fast worlds he has **no clear plan** beyond hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out of work with a **wedding** to pay.
whatWouldHelp: A boss who'd **train him** on the hands-on side, and **family** support.
